title: Detachment from things
hook: not owning nothing, but not being owned by things

segments.voice: Yesterday, muhasabah, the evening ledger, and your line: count before counted. Today, a rider in the shade.

A reed mat on a floor. That's the whole scene in a hadith from the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The Prophet ﷺ gets up from sleeping on it, and the weave has pressed marks into his side. His companions offer to make him a proper bed. His answer is a picture. What have I to do with this world? He is in it, he says, like a rider who stops in the shade of a tree, rests a while, then rides on and leaves the tree behind. Nothing about the tree is bad. The shade is real. But the rider doesn't move in.
screen: `A REED MAT, MARKS ON HIS SIDE.` → `A RIDER IN THE SHADE.` → `HE DOESN'T MOVE IN.`

segments.voice: The word is zuhd, usually put into English as renunciation, or detachment, and both can mislead. Renunciation sounds like an empty room and a cave. But another hadith in al-Tirmidhi defines zuhd in the world, starting with two things it is not. It is not making the lawful forbidden, and it is not throwing your wealth away. It's being more sure of what is in Allah's hand than of what is in your own hand. So zuhd isn't measured by what's in your house, but by where your heart is resting. A person with very little can be gripped by the little they have; a person with a lot can hold it loosely. The Qur'an names the test, in Pickthall's translation: "That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given." Read it as a gauge. If losing a thing would flatten you, and gaining it makes you giddy, it has a grip on you. If you can be glad of it and let it go, you own it, and it doesn't own you. A line people repeat in the tradition, without one sure source, says zuhd is not owning nothing, but being owned by nothing. And there's a promise. In the collection of Ibn Majah, a man asks for a deed that will make Allah and people love him. The answer: be detached from the world, and Allah will love you. Be detached from what people have, and people will love you.
screen: `NOT AN EMPTY ROOM.` · `MORE SURE OF ALLAH'S HAND THAN YOURS.` · `DON'T GRIEVE, DON'T GLOAT.` · then, large: `OWNED BY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Walk through your home in your mind and find one thing you haven't used in a long time but keep anyway. Notice the small tug that says, but what if I need it, and picture who could use it now: a neighbor, a shelter, a friend. If you pray, recall the rider in the shade; if not, let the picture of it leaving your hands sit for a moment.
Zuhd. Detachment: trusting what is in Allah's hand more than what is in your own, so that things can be enjoyed without taking hold of you. Today's word.
Your line: not owned by it. Glad of the shade, and still riding on. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers describe zuhd as an inner detachment rather than poverty: people keep their homes, work and wealth while trying to hold them loosely, and some practice it by regularly giving away what they no longer use.

chat.says: Does zuhd mean Muslims are supposed to give up everything they own?
options: No: it's being surer of what's in Allah's hand than your own, not owned by things.
Yes: true zuhd means making lawful things forbidden and living with nothing.
Yes: you should throw your wealth away, since owning anything is a sin.
